persona: Operations leaders responsible for how work gets done

room.title: Operations Leaders
room.description: How a head of operations redesigns the way a whole organisation runs — the operating cadence, where work is tracked, and the measures that show whether the change worked — with every team able to see the plan it's being asked to follow.

desks.title: Operating cadence redesign — forums, reporting and decisions
desks.description: Rebuilding the leadership operating rhythm: which recurring forums stay, merge or become written updates, the hours that frees, and how we'll know decisions are getting made faster.
desks.brief:
## Operating cadence redesign

**Organisation** Greythorn · 340 people, six departments, a leadership team of eight
**Sponsor** Naledi (CEO) · **Pilot** six weeks, review @+28d
**The problem** 577 hours a month in recurring forums, and a median of 12 days from an issue being raised to a decision

### What changes
- One **weekly business review** (WBR) replaces the monthly report pack and two cross-team syncs
- Department and project status meetings become **written updates**, posted the day before the WBR
- The exec meeting drops to 90 minutes and takes decisions, not updates
- Department monthly reviews halve, with a written pre-read
- A weekly **customer escalations review** gets its own 30 minutes instead of taking over other meetings

### What it should buy us
- 577 → 271 hours a month in recurring forums (306 freed, 53%)
- Decisions in 5 days, not 12
- One version of the numbers instead of nine monthly decks

### Where it stands
End of week 2 of the pilot. Written updates are landing on time from four of six departments, and the median time to a decision is down from 12 days to 9.

callout.title: Pilot: six weeks, then decide
callout.body: The new cadence runs for six weeks from @-14d. At the review @+28d we keep it only if median time to decision is under 7 days and department heads say written updates cost them less than the meetings did.

chart.title: Hours per month — before vs after

children.label: Written updates, day before the WBR
Do heads still read the updates?

blocks.p: Posted by end of day before the WBR. Five minutes to read, fifteen to write. If it takes longer, it's too long.

ol: **Numbers** — the three this department owns, against target
**Decisions needed** — what, from whom, by when
**Risks** — new, or worse since last week

ul: No slides, and no attachment without a one-line summary
Decisions needed go to the top of the WBR agenda
If nothing changed, write 'no change' — don't skip the week

blocks.p: Four of six departments posted on time both weeks. Field services and Procurement posted late — both say the Numbers section needs data they don't have until the morning of the WBR.

notes.title: What I heard from department heads
notes.body:
- Field services: the old monthly deck took most of a weekend; the written update takes 20 minutes — but the numbers need to land a day earlier
- Finance: likes the WBR; wants the ops & finance sync back for month-end week only
- Sales: worried the handoff meeting's relationships will fade without it — try a monthly lunch?
- PMO: project updates are shorter, but two project leads have stopped writing them

None of this is a reason to stop the pilot. The data timing is the one to fix first.

stickies.title: Pilot measures
stickies.body:
Hours in forums
Days from issue to decision
Updates on time
Heads' rating, 1–5

stickies.title: Don't
stickies.body: Don't add a meeting to fix a meeting.

desks.title: Work tracking consolidation — five trackers into one
desks.description: Moving project and request tracking out of five overlapping tools into one shared tracker, measured week by week: where projects live, hours spent copying status, and status meetings that disappear.
desks.brief:
## Work tracking consolidation — five trackers into one

**Scope** 142 active projects and requests across six teams
**Old homes** PMO's project tool, the operations master spreadsheet, the field services job board, CRM task lists, the old ticketing tool
**Target** @+28d — every active project in the shared tracker; two old tools cancelled at renewal

### Why
A project's status lived in up to three places. Project leads spent about 62 hours a week between them copying status from one tool into another, and 21 status meetings a week existed mostly to reconcile the copies.

### How we're moving
- **Pilot** with PMO and IT, then **wave 1** (operations, finance), then **wave 2** (sales handoffs, field services)
- New projects start in the shared tracker from day one; existing ones move when they next change stage
- Each old tracker has an owner and a retirement date

### Where it stands
112 of 142 projects are in the shared tracker. Copying is down to 17 hours a week and status meetings to 8. Two of the five old trackers are retired; the last 30 projects are in the PMO tool, the field services board and CRM tasks. Moving them by @+28d takes 7.5 a week; last week the old trackers went from 42 to 30.

callout.title: Measured, not assumed
callout.body: Copying hours come from a three-question pulse every Friday (41 of 48 project leads answered last week); status meetings are counted from the shared calendar. Target by @+28d: under 10 hours a week copying, and no project in more than one tool.

chart.title: Where projects live, week by week

children.label: Long projects finish where they started
Sales opens handoffs in the tracker
Status still asked for in DMs

ul: **PMO project tool** — 48 → 14 projects. Long-running projects finish there; read-only from @+21d, cancelled at renewal
**Field services job board** — 22 → 9. Crews move after the tablet rollout @+14d
**CRM task lists** — 18 → 7. Sales now opens delivery handoffs in the shared tracker
**Old ticketing tool** — 11 → 0. Request intake moved @-20d; the tool is switched off

blocks.p: Every active project lives in one place, every status question is answered with a link, and nobody copies status from one tool into another.

ul: Not migrating closed projects — each old tool stays read-only for a year, or exports them to the archive before it's cancelled
Not putting field crews on laptops — tablets first
Not adding fields 'just in case' — nine fields per project, agreed by all six teams

notes.title: Pulse comments — this week
notes.body:
From the 41 project leads who answered:

- 'Nobody has asked me for a status update in a week' (PMO)
- 'Still copying field jobs from the board into the tracker by hand' (operations — six people said this)
- 'Can sales see delivery dates without asking?' — yes, it's in the shared view; tell them
- 'Too many fields' — three people; we're at nine and holding the line

stickies.title: Renewals
stickies.body: PMO tool renews @+45d. Read-only from @+21d leaves more than three weeks' buffer.

stickies.title: Next
stickies.body:

2. Cancel the ticketing contract
3. Cut 3 more status meetings
